strengths: Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM) is an intuitive, well-motivated formulation that continuously balances imitation learning (DAgger) and reinforcement learning (PPO) based on policy entropy, avoiding brittle manual switching schedules.

Competitive performance on the HM3D-OVON benchmark val unseen split (40.1% SR, 20.9% SPL) using an RGB-only sensor setup without requiring depth sensors, odometry, or heavy vision-language foundation models during policy execution.
Solid empirical analysis of training dynamics, sample efficiency, and collision statistics in comparison to standard PPO, DAgger, and hard-switched schedules.
weaknesses: Potential data snooping / benchmark contamination during detector adaptation: Section 'Adaptation to predicted segmentation' and Section 3 of the Appendix describe calibrating confidence thresholds per category, and Figure 10 explicitly plots category-specific threshold sweeps on categories from the 'val unseen' split. In a true open-vocabulary setting, novel target categories are not known a priori to allow category-specific detector calibration.

Unclear exploration behavior under target absence: Table 11 demonstrates that providing an all-zero mask throughout the episode causes the policy to completely fail (0.1% SR). Since an agent in ObjectNav must explore unfamiliar scenes before encountering the target (during which time the detector output is an all-zero mask), it is unclear how the policy reliably executes search/exploration without being dependent on early false-positive or true-positive mask detections.

Marginal and conflicting impact of the auxiliary segmentation loss: In Table 3, introducing $\mathcal{L}_{seg}$ improves SR only marginally (from 69.3% to 70.4%) while degrading path efficiency (SPL drops from 40.8% to 39.4%) and substantially increasing collisions (from 14.5 to 18.8). Despite being claimed as a core contribution, the benefit of this auxiliary reconstruction loss remains questionable.

Using a DCGAN generator architecture to reconstruct the binary target mask as an auxiliary representation loss is unconventional, and the paper lacks ablation or justification comparing it against standard lightweight segmentation decoders (e.g., FPN or linear upsampling heads).

strengths: Principled and effective training scheduler (EALM): Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation provides an automatic, sample-level transition from DAgger imitation learning to PPO reinforcement learning based on policy uncertainty, eliminating brittle manual phase-switching schedules and cutting training sample complexity.

Strong empirical results on HM3D-OVON: The proposed method achieves competitive performance on the HM3D-OVON benchmark (40.1% SR, 20.9% SPL on val unseen) using only RGB sensor inputs, outperforming several baselines including methods utilizing depth and odometry.

Comprehensive ablation and safety analysis: The paper includes thorough comparisons of training strategies (Table 2), tracking both task performance (SR, SPL) and collision count as a critical proxy for agent safety and trajectory overfitting, supported by statistical significance testing.
weaknesses: Potential test-set tuning / leakage in detector threshold calibration: Section 'Adaptation to predicted segmentation' and Appendix Section 3 indicate that confidence thresholds of the YOLOE detector were calibrated per-category based on validation splits, including val unseen (e.g., Figure 10). In an open-vocabulary setting, per-category calibration on unseen evaluation categories is impractical and risks overfitting to the evaluation split. The paper should report performance using a single, globally fixed confidence threshold for all unseen categories.

Over-reliance on external detector and fragility to false negatives: Table 11 reveals that when the goal mask is absent (all zeros), success rate drops to 0.1%, showing that the policy is completely dependent on external detections and cannot navigate from RGB and text alone. Framing the method as a lightweight end-to-end policy is somewhat overstated given its total operational dependence on an external open-vocabulary segmentation model (YOLOE) running at inference.

Mixed benefits of the auxiliary segmentation loss: Table 3 indicates that adding the auxiliary segmentation loss (L_seg) produces a minor gain in SR (+1.1%) at the expense of reduced path efficiency (SPL drops from 40.8% to 39.4%) and increased collisions (from 14.5 to 18.8). The claim that this auxiliary task reliably disentangles representations is not clearly substantiated by these trade-offs.

Clarity on exploration behavior: Since the policy collapses to 0.1% SR when masks are absent (Table 11), it remains unclear how the agent performs multi-room exploration prior to first detecting the target object, as masks would typically be empty (all zeros) during this early phase.

strengths: Principled DAgger-to-PPO transition (EALM): The proposed Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation provides an intuitive and automated mechanism to blend imitation learning and reinforcement learning based on policy uncertainty, avoiding brittle manual stage scheduling and reducing training sample complexity.

Comprehensive empirical analysis: The submission provides thorough ablation studies covering training strategies, individual loss/observation components, collision metrics as safety proxies, training dynamics curves, and statistical significance testing.

Competitive benchmark performance: When integrated with open-vocabulary segmentation, the method achieves competitive results on the HM3D-OVON benchmark (40.1% SR on the Val Unseen split) compared to recent map-based and foundation model baselines.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation contamination via per-category threshold calibration: In Section 'Adaptation to predicted segmentation' and Table 4/Figure 10, the authors calibrate category-specific confidence thresholds for objects in the 'Val Unseen' split (yielding a jump from 35.1% to 40.1% SR). Tuning detector hyperparameters per category directly on the unseen evaluation split violates standard zero-shot/open-vocabulary evaluation protocols and artificially inflates generalization performance.

Misleading characterization of system independence and model footprint: The paper emphasizes a 'lightweight' (130M parameter) 'RGB-only' model operating without foundation models. However, at test time, navigation performance fundamentally depends on an external pretrained open-vocabulary detector/segmentor (YOLOE / YOLOv8-L). Neither the compute overhead, inference latency, nor parameter count of YOLOE is included in the policy comparison in Table 1.

Extreme policy brittleness without detector output: As shown in Table 11, when the binary goal mask is zeroed out and only the text instruction is available, performance drops to 0.1% SR. This indicates the policy has learned almost no multimodal grounding between text goals and raw RGB observations, functioning strictly as a downstream mask-tracker. If the upstream detector produces false negatives or fails, the policy completely breaks down.

Marginal and mixed utility of the auxiliary segmentation objective: Table 3 indicates that adding the auxiliary segmentation loss ($L_{seg}$) provides only an incremental gain in SR (69.3% to 70.4%) while degrading path efficiency (SPL drops from 40.8% to 39.4%) and increasing collisions (14.5 to 18.8). The architectural choice of using a DCGAN head for auxiliary mask decoding is also ad-hoc and inadequately justified compared to standard segmentation decoders.

strengths: Strong empirical performance on the challenging HM3D-OVON benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art results on val unseen (44.7% SR, 20.6% SPL) using RGB-only input without requiring depth, odometry, or massive vision-language models.

The proposed Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM) provides an elegant, well-motivated formulation to smoothly transition between imitation learning (DAgger) and reinforcement learning (PPO), eliminating brittle manual phase-switching schedules and demonstrating improved sample efficiency and safety in ablations.
Thorough evaluation and ablations, including systematic failure analysis (Table 5), training strategy comparisons (Table 2), component ablations (Table 3), and statistical significance testing.
Demonstration of real-world transfer on an iRobot Create 3 platform equipped with an onboard Jetson Orin PC, verifying real-time feasibility and practical deployment.
weaknesses: High sensitivity and dependency on the external open-vocabulary segmentation module: Table G shows that when only the text goal is provided (with a dummy zero mask), the success rate collapses completely to 0.1%. This reveals that the transformer policy has minimal standalone semantic grounding capability and essentially functions purely as a visual servoing policy conditioned on external segmentation masks.

Per-category confidence threshold calibration (Section 4.3 and Table 4) is required for optimal performance on known categories, which somewhat conflicts with the core spirit of open-vocabulary navigation where arbitrary novel textual queries may be specified at test time without prior tuning.

The collision frequency remains noticeably high (~45 collisions per episode on val unseen in Table 3 and 4, corresponding to approximately 9-10% of navigation steps), which poses safety concerns for real-world robotic deployment as acknowledged in the robot experiments (Appendix J).
Minor presentation issues, such as Table J reporting GPU memory usage as '3486 Gb' and '4992 Gb', which is evidently meant to be MB (or MiB).

strengths: Strong empirical results on the HM3D-OVON benchmark: achieving 44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL on the unseen validation split using only RGB observations, outperforming prior RGB-based policies and several methods equipped with depth and odometry.

Well-motivated Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM): dynamically schedules the transition between imitation learning (DAgger) and reinforcement learning (PPO) using action distribution entropy, effectively improving sample efficiency (reaching peak performance in ~200M steps vs. 300M for DAgRL) and avoiding catastrophic drops from manual switching.

Thorough ablation and failure analysis: the paper systematically evaluates individual contributions (EALM, goal mask encoding, auxiliary segmentation loss, semantic reward, threshold calibration, and fine-tuning) with rigorous statistical significance tests and failure mode categorizations.

Comprehensive exploration of the perception-policy interface: the study investigates realistic deployment considerations, including the impact of predicted vs. ground-truth masks, false positive/negative rates under lighting augmentations, latency benchmarks on edge hardware (Jetson Orin), and real-robot demonstrations.
weaknesses: Severe dependence on the target mask input: as shown in Table G, removing the goal mask during inference causes the policy to fail almost completely (0.1% SR), indicating that the policy functions primarily as a mask tracker rather than an autonomous open-vocabulary search-and-identification system.

Manual vocabulary and threshold curation: the performance gain from YOLOE adaptation heavily relies on calibrating per-class confidence thresholds and pruning synonyms (Section 4.3, Table 4). While practical, this compromises the fully autonomous zero-shot generalization promise when encountering arbitrary novel textual queries in the wild.

Increased collision rates after predicted-mask fine-tuning: fine-tuning on YOLOE predicted segmentations causes the collision rate to more than double (from 20.2 to 45.4 collisions per episode in Table 4), and the authors note unsafe stopping behavior on the physical robot.

Reporting and unit inconsistencies: in Table J, GPU memory is listed as '3486 Gb' and '4992 Gb', which is clearly an erroneous unit (likely MB or VRAM across a distributed cluster) and needs clarification.

strengths: Strong empirical performance: The proposed lightweight transformer model (130M parameters total) achieves state-of-the-art results on the challenging HM3D-OVON benchmark (44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL on val unseen), outperforming prior RGB-only baselines as well as methods that utilize depth, odometry, or much larger vision-language models.

Principled and practical training scheme: Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM) provides an elegant, automatic transition from demonstration-based bootstrapping (DAgger) to reinforcement learning (PPO) guided by policy entropy, eliminating fragile manual stage transitions, reducing sample complexity, and noticeably lowering collisions.

Effective bridge between ideal and predicted perception: The synergy between the auxiliary mask reconstruction loss, mask-area semantic reward, and detector adaptation effectively mitigates the severe performance drop when transitioning from ground-truth masks to noisy real-time open-vocabulary predictions (YOLOE).

Thorough ablation and empirical rigor: The paper provides extensive ablations analyzing loss components, switching strategies, threshold bounds, failure modes, statistical significance (paired t-tests in appendix), inference latency on embedded edge hardware (Jetson Orin), and preliminary real-robot transfer.
weaknesses: Practical scalability of detector threshold calibration: The method relies noticeably on per-category confidence threshold calibration and vocabulary cleaning (yielding +7.0% SR in Table 4). In true unconstrained open-vocabulary navigation where goal targets can be arbitrary novel phrases, manual calibration of confidence thresholds is less feasible.

Critical dependence on mask detection at test time: Table G demonstrates that providing zero masks causes the success rate to collapse to 0.1%, highlighting that the policy relies almost entirely on the external segmenter to locate and trigger navigation towards the goal, leaving the agent vulnerable when the segmentation model fails entirely.

Limited real-world quantitative evaluation: While the qualitative demonstration on the physical iRobot Create 3 (Appendix J) is appreciated, it is restricted to two anecdotal test setups, and the authors note persistent safety/collision risks near goals due to the lack of metric depth sensing.
Minor presentation inaccuracy: In Table J, the GPU Memory Usage is reported as '3486 Gb' and '4992 Gb', which is an obvious unit typo for megabytes (MB).
